questions.q: A student washes a wool sweater in hot water (60°C) with a regular alkaline detergent (pH 10.5) and agitates vigorously in a top-load machine. The sweater shrinks to half its size and feels stiff. Identify the TWO primary fibre-level mechanisms responsible for this damage.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) **Felting** — Wool scales interlock under heat, moisture, and mechanical agitation, causing irreversible shrinkage. (2) **Alkaline hydrolysis** — High pH cleaves peptide bonds in keratin, destroying fibre integrity and causing stiffness. A wrong answer (e.g., "wool melts" or "dye runs") reveals confusion between thermoplastic synthetic behaviour and protein fibre chemistry, or ignorance of pH-specific hydrolysis.

questions.q: Explain why cotton and linen can be boiled (100°C) with strong alkali (e.g., sodium carbonate) for stain removal, but silk and wool cannot. Use the terms "cellulosic", "protein", "hydrogen bonding", and "peptide bond" in your explanation.
questions.a: Correct answer: Cotton/linen are **cellulosic** polymers with extensive **hydrogen bonding** that stabilises the structure at high temperature and resists alkali; alkali swells cellulose, aiding soil release. Silk/wool are **protein** fibres held by **peptide bonds** and disulfide cross-links; alkali hydrolyses peptide bonds, and heat + moisture disrupts hydrogen bonds in the amorphous regions, causing permanent damage. A wrong answer that omits peptide bond hydrolysis or claims "silk is delicate" without chemical reasoning shows surface-level memorisation.

questions.q: A polyester shirt has an oily food stain. The student washes it in cold water (20°C) with a non-ionic surfactant detergent, but the stain remains. Propose a corrected laundering protocol (temperature, detergent type, mechanical action) and justify each change using polyester's fibre properties.
questions.a: Correct protocol: (1) **Warm water (40–50°C)** — Polyester is thermoplastic (Tg ~70°C); warm water lowers oil viscosity and increases surfactant efficiency without risking heat-setting wrinkles. (2) **Heavy-duty detergent with builders + non-ionic/anionic mix** — Polyester is oleophilic; builders sequester hardness ions, non-ionics emulsify oil better at moderate temps. (3) **Moderate agitation** — Polyester has high tenacity and resists abrasion; mechanical action aids oily soil removal. A wrong answer using cold water or soap-only shows misunderstanding of polyester's oleophilia and the temperature-dependence of non-ionic surfactant cloud point.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the ironing requirements for linen and silk. Include: maximum safe temperature, moisture condition, pressing technique, and the fibre-property reason for each.
questions.a:
Correct comparison:
| Parameter | Linen (Cellulosic) | Silk (Protein) |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| Max temp  | 200–230°C (cotton/linen setting) | 110–150°C (silk/wool setting) |
| Moisture  | **Damp** (steam iron) — water plasticises cellulose, allows hydrogen bond reformation under pressure | **Dry or slightly damp** — excess moisture + heat causes water spotting and weakens wet silk (loss of H-bonds in amorphous regions) |
| Technique | Firm pressure, gliding — high wet strength tolerates pressure | Light pressure, lift-and-press — low wet strength, risk of yarn slippage and shine |
| Reason    | Cellulose chains reorient via H-bonds when damp + heat + pressure | Protein chains degrade via hydrolysis at high temp; moisture swells fibre, causing distortion under pressure |
A wrong answer that irons silk damp on high heat reveals confusion between cellulosic and protein fibre responses to thermo-mechanical treatment.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Since synthetic fibres like nylon and polyester are strong and durable, they can be washed and dried at the highest machine settings without damage." Provide three specific counter-arguments based on fibre physics/chemistry.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The statement is **false**. Three counter-arguments: (1) **Thermoplasticity** — Nylon (Tm ~220°C) and polyester (Tm ~260°C) soften well below boiling; tumble-dry high (70–80°C) can cause heat-setting of wrinkles, shrinkage, or melting at contact points. (2) **Oleophilia** — Synthetics attract oily soils; high heat can bake oils into fibres, making stains permanent. (3) **Static & pilling** — High mechanical action + heat increases fibre-to-fibre friction, generating static and promoting pill formation on low-modulus synthetics. A wrong answer that agrees reveals ignorance of glass transition/melting behaviour and oleophilic soil retention.

questions.q: Design a single "universal" laundering protocol (one wash cycle, one dry cycle, one iron setting) that would safely clean a mixed load of: 60% cotton / 40% polyester blend kurta, 100% linen napkin, and 100% acrylic sweater. Specify all parameters and justify why this protocol is the **maximum common safe envelope** — then explain why the acrylic sweater still risks damage.
questions.a: Universal safe protocol: **Wash:** 30°C, neutral pH liquid detergent (non-ionic dominant), gentle cycle (low agitation, short duration). **Dry:** Flat air-dry in shade (no tumble). **Iron:** 110°C (synthetic/wool setting), dry press with cloth. Justification: 30°C protects acrylic (Tg ~85°C, but heat-setting starts lower) and silk/wool if present; neutral pH protects protein fibres and avoids cellulose degradation at extremes; low agitation prevents felting (wool) and pilling (acrylic). Acrylic risk: **Pilling** — even gentle agitation can cause surface fibre breakage on low-tenacity acrylic, and flat drying may not prevent distortion if the knit is heavy. A poor answer that suggests 40°C or tumble-dry low shows failure to identify the most restrictive fibre (acrylic/protein) as the limiting factor.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Fibre-specific laundering is the systematic ______ of tailored cleaning, drying, and finishing procedures for cotton, linen, wool, silk, and synthetic fibres based on their distinct physical morphology, chemical reactivity, and structural responses to water, heat, mechanical action, and chemical agents.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have a laundry basket containing a white cotton kurta, a linen tablecloth, a wool sweater, a silk dupatta, and a ______ sports T-shirt — all soiled.
What is Fibre-specific laundering? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Fibre-specific laundering is the systematic application of tailored cleaning, drying, and finishing procedures for cotton, linen, wool, silk, and synthetic fibres based on their distinct physical morphology, chemical reactivity, and structural responses to water, heat, mechanical action, and chemical agents.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Now, for each fibre, decide: (______) Can it withstand hot water?
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Fibre-specific laundering?
questions.a: Misconception: "Natural fibres are always more delicate than synthetics, so synthetics can take harsher treatment." Why it's wrong: This conflates "natural" with "delicate".

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently design a complete laundering protocol (sorting, detergent selection, wash temperature, mechanical action, drying method, ironing temperature) for any given garment made of cotton, linen, wool, silk, polyester, nylon, or acrylic, justifying each step with the underlying fibre property.
